problem: Earlier instruction-following systems on the SAIL route-instruction benchmark map free-form navigation instructions to actions only with hand-built linguistic machinery: semantic parsers (CCG, PCFG), seed or logical-form lexicons, and discriminative re-rankers. None of them learns the whole language-to-action mapping end-to-end from raw instruction/action pairs.
motivation: Robots such as voice-commanded wheelchairs or micro aerial vehicles need to follow ambiguous, error-ridden free-form route instructions. Task-specific linguistic resources limit how well such systems generalize. Neural encoder-decoder models with attention had just succeeded in machine translation and image captioning, which suggests the instruction-to-action problem could also be learned directly as sequence-to-sequence translation conditioned on the observable world state.
key_idea: Treat instruction following as sequence-to-sequence translation: a bidirectional LSTM encodes the instruction, a multi-level attention aligner attends over both raw word embeddings and encoder hidden states, and an LSTM decoder conditioned on the current observed world state emits actions until 'stop'.
insight:
No component relies on linguistic priors, yet the model sets a new single-sentence SOTA on SAIL, so parsers and lexicons are not needed when attention can ground words to landmarks. The ablations in Table 2 (single-sentence / multi-sentence) show where the gains come from:
- Removing the encoder (word embeddings fed straight to the attention) causes the largest drop: 69.98→61.63 and 26.07→16.67. Sentence-level context is needed to disambiguate phrases such as 'turn right before' vs 'after'.
- Attending only over high-level states instead of multi-level: 69.98→68.09 and 26.07→24.79. Low-level word identities (e.g. 'easel') help match landmarks in the world state.
- Replacing learned attention with uniform attention: 68.05 and 25.04.
- A unidirectional encoder: 67.44 and 24.50.
In the distance evaluation (Table 3), single-sentence accuracy rises from 71.73 to 86.62 when ending within 1 node of the goal counts. Most failures are therefore near-misses.
method: Bidirectional LSTM encoder: one-hot words x_j are encoded forward and backward, and the annotation h_j concatenates the forward and backward LSTM states.

Multi-level aligner (attention): the context z_t = Σ_j α_tj [x_j; h_j] combines the raw word vector and the encoder state. The weights are a softmax over β_tj = vᵀ tanh(W s_{t-1} + U x_j + V h_j), a one-layer perceptron.

World-state representation: the local line-of-sight observation y_t is a concatenation of bag-of-words vectors (floor patterns, wall paintings, objects) for the forward, left and right directions, with no hand-engineered features.
LSTM decoder with deep output layer: it takes E·y_t, z_t and s_{t-1}, computes q_t = L0(E y_t + Ls s_t + Lz z_t), and applies a softmax over the next action.

Training: per-step negative log-likelihood of the demonstrated action, optimized with Adam. Early stopping uses the validation task metric, because validation log-likelihood correlates poorly with accuracy. Only hidden size and dropout are tuned.

Inference: beam search with width 10 over an ensemble of 10 randomly initialized models, using averaged posteriors. Multi-sentence inference runs sentence-by-sentence, and each new sentence's beam is initialized with the previous k best hypotheses.

setting.backbone: Bidirectional LSTM encoder + multi-level attention aligner + LSTM decoder (trained from scratch, ensemble of 10)
setting.training_data: SAIL route-instruction corpus (MacMahon et al. 2006): 706 instruction paragraphs over 126 start/end pairs in 3 virtual worlds, segmented into single-sentence/action pairs (~2000 training pairs). Three-fold cross-validation over maps: train on 2 maps, split 90/10 train/val, test on the held-out map. No extra data.
setting.observation: symbolic local line-of-sight world state: bag-of-words of visible floor patterns, wall paintings and objects for the forward/left/right directions
setting.action_space: discrete symbolic actions on the hallway/intersection graph (e.g. go forward one segment, turn left/right, stop)
setting.simulator: SAIL virtual worlds (MacMahon, Stankiewicz, and Kuipers 2006)
setting.privileged: perfect symbolic perception of visible landmarks (no raw vision); otherwise none

numbers_note:
The SAIL benchmark is evaluated by three-fold cross-validation over its three maps, with results as a size-weighted average over held-out test maps. 'test' denotes the held-out map, not an official test split. Ablation variants (Table 2) are not listed as entries:
- single-sentence: High-level Aligner 68.09, No Aligner 68.05, Unidirectional 67.44, No Encoder 61.63
- multi-sentence: 24.79, 25.04, 24.50, 16.67
Footnote 5 claims the non-ensemble model is still SOTA but gives no numbers.
results: On SAIL single-sentence the model reaches 69.98 (vDev) and 71.05 (vTest) accuracy, a new SOTA over Artzi & Zettlemoyer 2013 (65.28) and Artzi, Das & Petrov 2014 (64.36). It uses no parsers, lexicons or re-rankers and clearly beats the CRF aligner of Andreas & Klein 2015 (59.60). Multi-sentence accuracy is 26.07 (vDev) and 30.34 (vTest). This beats Chen & Mooney 2011, Chen 2012 and Kim & Mooney 2012, but stays below Artzi et al. 2014 (35.44) and Artzi & Zettlemoyer 2013 (31.93), which use extra lexicon annotation.
limitations: The world state is a clean symbolic bag-of-words of visible landmarks in small synthetic grid worlds, with no raw perception or continuous control.
Multi-sentence accuracy trails the best parser-based methods (30.34 vs 35.44) because of the very small paragraph-level training data and cascading errors across sentences.
Headline numbers depend on a 10-model ensemble plus beam search. The vTest setting uses the test map for early stopping, which is optimistic.
